exact_source_context.626_section2_convention: \textbf{2.2.} Désormais, on suppose que \(k\) est algébriquement clos, que \(X\) est projectif, muni d'un faisceau inversible très ample \(H={O}_X(1)\) et que \(X\) est intègre, de dimension \(r\).
exact_source_context.638_reduction: Dans la d\'emonstration de la premi\`ere partie de 3.8, on s'est ramen\'e au cas o\`u \(S\) est int\`egre et \(Y\) est normal et int\`egre sur \(S\), donc \(Y\) est int\`egre. Si \(\varphi=0\), alors \(X=Y\) et l'assertion est triviale. Sinon, quitte \`a restreindre \(S\), on peut supposer que pour tout \(s\in S\), on a \(\varphi_s\ne0\), donc \(\varphi_s\) est \({O}_{Y_s}\)-r\'egulier et la dimension \(r\) de \(Y_s\) est \(\ge3\).
exact_source_context.639_statement_and_proof:
\textbf{Lemme 3.11.} \emph{Soient \(k\) un corps alg\'ebriquement clos, \(Y\) un \(k\)-sch\'ema normal, projectif muni d'un faisceau ample \({O}_Y(1)\), et \(X\) le sch\'ema des z\'eros d'une section \(\varphi\) de \({O}_Y(1)\). On suppose que \(Y\) soit de dimension \(\ge3\) (resp. \(\ge2\)). Alors le morphisme \(\Pic_{Y/k}\longrightarrow\Pic_{X/k}\) (resp. le morphisme \(\Pic^\tau_{Y/k}\to\Pic^\tau_{X/k}\) (voir 4.1)) est de type fini et a un noyau \(N\) qui est un groupe fini (non-r\'eduit en g\'en\'eral).}

En effet, on peut \'evidemment supposer \(\varphi\ne0\)\,; donc \(\varphi\) est r\'eguli\`ere, \(Y\) \'etant int\`egre. Le morphisme envisag\'e est de type fini gr\^ace \`a la premi\`ere partie de 3.8 (resp. gr\^ace \`a 4.7 (iii)). Par suite le noyau \(N\) est un groupe alg\'ebrique, donc contenu dans \(\Pic^\tau_{Y/k}\), donc est le m\^eme

governing_convention_outcome: Folio616 introduces an algebraically closed field k and projective k-scheme X with an ample invertible sheaf; it does not impose integrality.
Section2.2 on626 says that from now on k is algebraically closed and X is integral projective of dimension r. This fixes the named X in the technical-lemma section.

Section3 begins new quantified scheme/functor statements on631. Its later statements independently introduce X and Y over an arbitrary noetherian S. No exposé-wide convention normal=integral, connectedness, or pure dimension is declared in the read source context.

Theorem3.8 on637 explicitly requires the dimension bound for each irreducible component of each intersection X_s∩Y_s^i. Its proof reduces Y to normal and integral over S;638 explicitly uses that integrality and obtains fiber dimension≥3.

Lemma3.11 on639 reintroduces an algebraically closed field k and a normal projective k-scheme Y with an ample sheaf. Its printed first dimension condition is dimY≥3; no connected, integral or componentwise qualifier is written in that local statement. Its proof then calls Y integral.

The immediate use within the preceding proof concerns integral geometric fibers, so the counterexample below does not refute that intended local application. It refutes the standalone first branch under the literal aggregate-dimension reading. The context is recorded rather than replaced by a new hypothesis.

counterexample.ample_sheaf: The restriction of O_{P^5}(1) along the disjoint closed embeddings of the two complementary linear subspaces P(k^4) and P(k^2) in P(k^4⊕k^2); it restricts to O(1) on each component and is very ample.
counterexample.section: Choose a nonzero coordinate linear form on each component. The resulting global section phi has zero scheme X=P^2_k disjoint-union Spec k.
counterexample.hypotheses: Every local ring of Y belongs to one smooth projective-space component and is normal. Y is projective, normal, and has dimension max(3,1)=3. The section is regular on both components.
counterexample.map: Restriction f*:Pic(Y)→Pic(X) sends the invertible sheaf L_b=(O_{P^3},O_{P^1}(b)) to (O_{P^2},O_{Spec k}) for every integer b.
counterexample.injective_kernel_family: The assignment b↦[L_b] is an injective group homomorphism Z→ker(f*). Tensor products add b. If L_b≃L_c, restriction to P^1 gives O(b-c)≃O; its divisor degree is b-c, whereas a principal divisor has degree0, so b=c.
counterexample.conclusion: The kernel has infinitely many k-points. A finite k-group scheme has finite underlying topological space and, over algebraically closed k, finitely many k-points. Therefore this kernel is not finite, even allowing nonreduced finite groups.
counterexample.componentwise_comparison: On the P^1 component, X∩P^1 is a point of dimension0, so this example fails exactly the explicit componentwise≥2 condition in3.8. Its P^3 component meets the bound with P^2.
